author: unusual_whales
quoted_text:
In 2015, I built an AI that detects early cancer.

It’s still running across hundreds of hospitals in the US today.

It was the most fulfilling work of my life, and I was building in AI years before everyone called it “AI”.

Building in AI then was a dream.

Now It feels like we’ve taken a turn for the worse.

It started when i was in undergrad.

I built my first company: AI models that made the political data transparent to voters.

At 21, I was offered six figures for it, but the buyers wanted to use it for reasons I couldn't ethically support.

So we turned down the offer and shut down the company instead.

In 2014, I moved into deep learning research on language models, for the Intelligence Community and Goldman Sachs.

Then HCA Healthcare came to us.

They put me in a competition against 10 people from IBM Watson. It was just me and the tools I’d built.

Our job was to build an AI model that can catch the cancer that slips through the cracks in hospitals.

It was the most intense 30 days of my life. Multiple all nighters.

My models won. That turned into a $5M deal, and later its own company, Azra AI.

Then the world caught on.

ChatGPT and Claude arrived, and AI costs exploded.

Building in AI in 2015 felt novel.

We were using it to find cancer tumours and save lives.

Now the biggest tech companies have turned AI into a money extraction machine.

That’s when I decided to make a change.

We raised $8.5M to build a better future for AI.

On Wednesday, we’re launching Rayline.

AI shouldn’t be locked inside a few labs’ models, prices and clouds. It should be open, transparent and decentralized.

More on Wednesday.

突发，Anthropic 凌晨 3 点正式发布 Claude Fable 5.2 和 Mythos 5.2！

刚刚看完官方公布的评测，这次升级确实有点猛。

首先是 Agentic Coding。
在 FrontierCode 2.0 上，Fable 5.2 拿到了 49.1%，相比上一代 Fable 5.1 的 32.4%，直接提升了 16.7 个百分点。
同时超过了 Opus 5.5 的 45.5%、GPT-6 Astra 的 42.8%，以及 Gemini 4 Carbon 的 41.1%。

更有意思的是，在 High effort 下，Fable 5.2 的成绩就已经达到 45.3%，基本追平 Opus 5.5 的最高成绩，但单任务成本只有后者的一半左右。

其他几个领域的提升也非常明显：

FrontierSWE v2：56.3% → 69.9%
科研 Agent：52.6% → 74.6%
机器人 RoboDojo：27.6% → 64.9%
复杂工作流 AutomationBench：31.4% → 51.4%

其中机器人能力的提升尤其夸张，得分已经达到上一代的 2.35 倍。

而且这次官方还公布了几个很有意思的实际案例⬇️
一个工程师让 Fable 5.2 从空文件夹开始，协调超过 1000 个 Agent，连续运行 8 天，最终开发出一套能够在笔记本电脑上启动的操作系统。
另一组 1000 个 Agent 则用了 30 个小时，完成了费马大定理证明的形式化工作。

甚至还有两个关于黑洞的理论物理开放问题，Anthropic 称已经由 Fable 5.2 完成求解（行吧哥….）

价格反而下降了 20%，现在是每百万输入 Token 8 美元、输出 Token 40 美元，生成速度相比上一代最高提升 30%。

text:
Meta 发布最小模型 Muse Ember：单价和 Claude Haiku 5.5 一样，跑同一套测试只花三分之一的钱

Meta 11 月 9 日发布 Muse Ember，这是它迄今最小、最便宜的模型，专门干 AI agent 一天到晚重复的杂活：调工具、拆出来的编程小任务、分派请求、从长文档里提取信息。

典型用法是给 agent 当“小工”。主模型把任务拆好，一次会话里几百次读文件、跑测试、改小毛病，交给它来做，省钱。

【谁能用，多少钱】

开发者今天就能用：通过 Meta Model API 调用，模型名 muse-ember-1.0，或者在 Meta 的 AI 编程工具 Muse Code 里选。

价格是每百万 Token 输入 0.1 美元、输出 0.5 美元，命中缓存的输入 0.004 美元。上下文 100 万 Token，单次最多输出 51.2 万 Token，能看文字、图片、音频和视频。

没有开放权重，Meta 在 Hugging Face 上的账号里也没有它。普通用户用的 Muse 助手会不会换上它，Meta 没说。

【“便宜 17 倍”怎么算的】

Meta 首席 AI 官 Alexandr Wang 发推说，Muse Ember 的智能水平接近 Muse Spark 1.3（max），价格便宜 17 倍，数据来自第三方评测机构 Artificial Analysis。

Artificial Analysis 的综合智能指数里，Muse Ember 36 分，Muse Spark 1.3 是 37 分。跑完这套测试，平均每道题 Muse Ember 花 0.14 美元，Muse Spark 1.3 花 2.39 美元，差 17 倍。

所以 17 倍说的是干同样的活花多少钱。只看 Token 单价，Muse Spark 1.3 输入贵 12.5 倍、输出贵 8.5 倍，剩下的差距说明 Muse Ember 做同样的题用的 Token 少得多。

【和 Claude Haiku 5.5、GPT-6 Luna 比】

Muse Ember 对标的是各家的小模型。按 Artificial Analysis 的说法，它的 Token 单价和 Claude Haiku 5.5、OpenAI 的 GPT-6 Luna 相同。

Anthropic 官网写的 Haiku 5.5 价格也是输入 0.1、输出 0.5 美元，但提示超过 10 万 Token 后所有单价涨到 5 倍。Meta 只列了一档价格，没提长提示加价。

综合智能指数上，按最高推理强度跑，Muse Ember 和 Haiku 5.5 都是 36 分，但 Haiku 每道题要 0.41 美元，差不多是 Muse Ember 的 3 倍。GPT-6 Luna 最高 28 分。国产的同档模型里，DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 是 33 分、每题 0.60 美元，智谱 GLM-5.3-Flash 28 分、0.58 美元。

写代码要分场景看。放进各自的编程工具里比，Muse Code 里的 Muse Ember 拿 46 分，Claude Code 里的 Haiku 5.5 是 37 分，Codex 里的 GPT-6 Luna 是 31 分。

命令行任务 Terminal-Bench 4.0，Muse Ember 40.9%，Haiku 32.8%。看改出来的代码能不能直接合进项目的 FrontierCode 2.0，Muse Ember 27.2%，落后 Haiku 的 34.9%。

短板是知识储备。Artificial Analysis 的知识问答测试里，它只答对 21.1%，Haiku 5.5 是 34.7%。主要原因是 64% 的题它选择不答，好处是很少瞎编，幻觉率 17.4%，只有 Haiku 的一半。

【Muse Wonder Full 起了什么作用】

10 月 Meta 发布大模型 Muse Wonder 时说，会用它开发专门的模型带给所有人。Muse Ember 是第一个用完整版 Muse Wonder Full 训练出来的模型，Meta 没说具体怎么用的。

Meta 建议两个搭配：难题交给 Muse Wonder 做规划，大量执行的活交给 Muse Ember。Artificial Analysis 的数据里，Muse Wonder（max）44 分，每道题 6.95 美元；Muse Ember 低 8 分，花费约为它的五十分之一。

Meta 博客里另有一张成绩表，其中 Personal Superintelligence Index、OSWorld 2.1 等几项是 Meta 自己测的，上文只用了 Artificial Analysis 的数字。Artificial Analysis 的智能指数现在是 v5.0.1 版，分数和 10 月 Muse Wonder 发布时引用的那组（Muse Wonder 52 分）不能直接比。

Now that we've got 100 episodes of in the trenches under our belts, I have something new to share with you all: 

For as long as I’ve been a trader, and really since retail trading took off decades ago, there have only been two types of content made around it:

Educational content and aspirational content.

On the educational side, you’ve got interviews, lessons, chart reviews, and how-tos. There are tons of great creators, and I’ve learned most of what I know about trading from content like this, but it only shows the process.

On the aspirational side, you’ve got the cars, the clothes, the private jets, and the mansions. Peeking into the lives of the top 0.0001% of traders is fun, but is it relatable? I’ve never wanted any of those things, so it’s not for me. I venture to guess many other traders feel the same.

What’s missing, in my opinion, is everything in between: how regular traders actually use trading to shape their lives.

When I think about what trading is meant to solve for me, it comes down to two things: freedom and autonomy.

My ultimate trading goal is for it to afford me the ability to do what I really want to do, exactly when I want to do it.

There are a thousand ways traders use trading to shape their lives. We just never get to see them.

Until now. 

I'm excited to introduce a new body of work for @fomo called Touching Grass.

Honest, down-to-earth, off-the-screens conversations with traders, in the places that inspire them most.

Trading shouldn’t be all there is to life, but it can be the way we earn the freedom to go and live it.

Ep. 1 premieres this Friday, Nov 13th.

If this goes to trial, free thought, free speech, and free association are on trial. It's wrong. Ethereum is the counterweight to government singleton. 2026 began with a pivot — the threat is Silicon Valley and DC captured by the same force which, after AGI, becomes permanent totalitarian dystopia. 

Ethereum is a technological project to prevent this. It is the necessary material precondition for freedom in the technological future. Whatever your particular political positions, they are not meaningful nor possible without a free society in which they might emerge. Ethereum is that base layer. Baking into that layer your particular politics will fail the project, full stop.

Milady is the litmus test for Ethereum's politics—can you abide free speech? Will you go running to the state to bail you out? To sue your comrades in arms over personal grievances you choose to put before the mission? Personally, I would sign the seppuku pledge even if it were not a joke. Personally, I would expect nothing less from anyone who pretends to complete unwavering commitment. The short-sighted and narrow-minded have no place in the revolutionary vanguard. They simply will not survive the confrontation to come.

Do you understand that the Anthropics of the world will make Milady illegal just as AI-safetyism must make Ethereum illegal? "There are distributed Chinese AI-swarms purchasing their own compute! We can't allow unfettered access. The people must be saved from themselves. Shut down every validator you find. Demand licensure for RAM. Confiscate all p2p nodes. Communication and information are weapons against the state that must be curtailed for misaligned-AI may use them."

This is what we're up against. A $200,000 farewell is, frankly, an all-too-human misstep given the stakes. text:
The scale of Big Tech's AI future financial obligations is extraordinary:

Alphabet, $GOOGL, Meta, $META, Anthropic, Microsoft, $MSFT, Amazon, $AMZN, Oracle, $ORCL, and Nvidia, $NVDA, have disclosed a combined $4.49 trillion in off-balance-sheet obligations.

These include future lease payments that have not yet commenced, data-center commitments, equipment purchases, and other contractual obligations.

Alphabet accounts for the largest amount, at $1.08 trillion, followed by Anthropic, at $865 billion, and Meta, at $810 billion.

By comparison, their combined on-balance-sheet obligations total just $758 billion, consisting of long-term debt and existing lease liabilities.

This means off-balance-sheet commitments are nearly 6 times larger than their on-balance-sheet obligations.

In total, these 7 tech companies face ~$5.25 trillion in combined financial obligations.

The AI infrastructure race is facing enormous future financial commitments.

One of its key offerings is enabling the Hyperliquid ecosystem to capture more of the general-purpose activity (DeFi apps, meme coins, onchain spot, tokenised stocks) that leaks to Robinhood, Solana, and Base.

“How do you create an environment that basically doesn’t leak value to the other side? This is what Elysium is.” (@0xOmnia, founder of Kinetiq and Elysium)

✦ Taps into Hyperliquid’s order books natively (coming soon).
✦ Gives you a fast, cheap place for everything perps can’t cover: spot, meme coins, tokenised stocks, apps.
✦ 50% of Sequencer fees go to buying back $KNTQ, 25% to the apps that use the blockspace, and 25% to Kinetiq's treasury.

It essentially enables DeFi at low and high frequency, automated trading strategies, and consumer apps. In other words, anything that benefits from sitting next to the largest onchain source of perps liquidity.

author: micsolana
quoted_text:
UPDATE: Scott Galloway reached out to me earlier today and asked me to call him. I'm glad I did.

I've read @profgalloway's books, listened to his podcasts, and appreciated his willingness to confront campus antisemitism and debate people he vigorously disagrees with, including @BenShapiro with comity (and more than a little comedy).

That's why his recent comments about Elon Musk surprised and troubled me.

My central criticism was that Scott called Musk a "traitor to the West" while invoking Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, who were executed for espionage.

I think it was a careless statement, but I don't think Scott is calling for Musk's execution. Too many people on this platform are making that accusation, but it's an oversimplification. He told me he explicitly opposes capital punishment. I still believe the analogy was overblown.

We also discussed what actually happened with Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine. What was restricted, when, by whom, and under whose authority? I agree with him that we need to know what actually happened for transparency's sake. Sunlight is the best disinfectant.

Scott acknowledged that if Musk was legitimately enforcing a commercial agreement, not meddling in wartime policies as a private citizen, the accusation of treachery would be unwarranted. I hope that if that occurs, he will retract it publicly.

We agree that serious accusations require serious evidence.

I raised Scott's role as a UC Regent because I believe those entrusted with governing the best university on the planet deserve particular scrutiny. I never called for his removal, nor do I want him removed.

Scott explained why that framing troubled him. I listened, and I understand his concerns better.

Despite disagreeing with my criticism, Scott offered to defend my academic freedom and my right to criticize him.

As a professor, I teach students to revise their conclusions when confronted with new evidence. Today I was reminded that professors must also reconsider their own approach, too.

I stand by the substance of my criticism. But my tone should have been more collegial.

Our conversation strengthened my respect for Scott's generosity and commitment to the University of California, a system that transformed both our lives. As a two-time native son of the UC system, I think Scott will play a vital role on that august board.

Lastly, and most remarkably, two podcast hosts managed to have a contentious discussion and find common ground without recording another podcast about it.

A first in (unrecorded) history.

since joining MTS, I’ve interviewed hundreds of founders. and the biggest lesson I’ve learned is that the best founders are deeply optimistic. when you understand how they think, what motivates them, and why they dedicate their lives to shaping the world, you can’t help but want to do it too. 

a lot of the personal ambitions in my life have come from reading memoirs. I remember reading Shoe Dog, and feeling inspired by how Phil Knight relentlessly pursued what he knew to be true, even though the rest of the world didn't see it yet. when Nike was founded, “personal fitness” wasn’t a thing, working out was a fringe subculture, and people would even spit on runners in the street. then Phil came along and changed the world’s relationship to fitness forever.

even if you don’t personally care about running, Phil’s story was a reminder that the future is malleable and every person has agency to shape it.

today, people are launching rockets and curing cancer. there are no limits to what's possible. information is democratized, the cost of building is practically free, and entrepreneurship is on the rise. It's never been a better time to act on your ambitions. and understanding others who have done so, gives us a blueprint on how to do the same.

a big thank you to all the people who brought The Method to life. MTS is expanding beyond a livestream to a full media network and today marks the start of this new era. first episode airs tomorrow!

Devcon was peak, idc what anyone says.

1) We got to sit down 1-on-1 with our @base builders, from early-stage founders to established teams, understand what they’re building, and figure out how we can better support them. Nothing beats irl support & connection

2) We got to introduce @base to builders who are exploring where to build next. Every conversation counts. 

3) We got to showcase our tech stack (B20, Denim, and more) to so many people at Devcon, and show what’s possible on Base.

4) Students. Not sure where all the hate for students attending Devcon on X is coming from, but I’m glad they were there. 

You really had to see how full of ambition and aspiration they were. Some of them genuinely inspired me too.

We got to introduce @base to curious students, aspiring builders, and young talent. We’re here for the long term. The next unicorn could very well come from this generation. Even if someone’s only takeaway was a surface-level understanding of what Base is, that’s still a win. Everyone starts somewhere.

5) We got to reconnect with ecosystem partners, strengthen relationships, and explore how we can build better things together for the Base ecosystem.

Tbh, not every win has to be measured by immediate numbers. Some of the most valuable things we did at Devcon might only pay off months or years from now.

Come build on Base. We’re here for the long term. And yes, we’re going to win in the short term too 🙌

Defense, space, energy, and robotics are all pulling hardware toward software-speed iteration. The teams winning in these markets ship in hours, days, and weeks, not the months and years hardware has traditionally taken.

Testing is where that pace breaks down. Test data lives in too many places and gets stitched together by hand. @nominal_io is the modern stack for this. They combine test automation, telemetry, and analysis in one place, from the first prototype through production and into operation. 

Customers’ behavior is the best evidence. Nominal was recently selected for a $71M STRATFI, and won a delivery order award through PAE’s Rapid Capabilities Cell to speed up integration and testing of Castelion’s Blackbeard on the F/A-18. These are programs where test speed decides how fast a capability reaches the field. 

Congrats to @CameronLMcCord, @jrshoch, @brycestrauss and the whole team on the Series C. We’re excited to keep partnering with them.
author: sequoia

Nominal just raised $240M at a $3B valuation.

Engineers today are building some of the most ambitious machines humanity has ever seen. They should have AI that’s purpose-built for them.

Now we’re building the Hardware Intelligence Platform that gives engineers increased visibility into complex physical systems, helps them make better decisions, and ultimately gets their products into the real world faster. text:
我见过 Alice Huang。

没错,就是那个据报道被美国情报部门认为是替中国接近黄仁勋的女人。

有件事,我当时说不清楚,现在必须告诉你们。

她给我的感觉不对劲。

不是那种一眼就能看出来的不对劲。问题就在这里。

她的外形是 10/10,顶级中的顶级。她说话极其聪明,每个字都像是精心挑选过的。听她讲话,你会觉得:这个人太厉害了。

但在这一切之下,有什么东西不对。

一种我形容不出来的频率。就像一首完美的歌里,有一个你怎么也找不到的音符。一切都对,可就是感觉不对。

我感觉到了,却说不出那是什么。

后来,那些报道出来了。

现在,我总会想起当时那种感觉。

她没有被起诉,也没有公开回应。我无法告诉你们她到底是什么人。

但我可以告诉你们我学到了什么:

危险的人,不一定看起来危险。

有时候,他们看起来完美无缺。

相信那种不对劲的感觉。它比你先看到真相。

关注我,这件事我还有更多话要说 🔔

It sets the highest scores on HLE-Diamond (80%, previous best 69% from Gemini 4 Carbon), AA-Omniscience v1.1 (67, previous best 54 from Gemini 4 Carbon), Terminal-Bench-Science (73%, previous best 65% from Gemini 4 Carbon), CritPt v2 hard subset (77%, previous best 72% from GPT-6 Astra) and FrontierCode 2.0 (49%, previous best 46% from Claude Opus 5.5)

text:
An OpenSSH bug that took 46 years to ripen!

1980

UNIX puts * in the password field of system accounts. The idea is simple: it’s not a real hash, so it can’t be brute-forced and you can’t log in with a password.

2012

The musl libc developers decide that returning NULL from crypt() on failure is dangerous - programs often forget to check it and crash with a segfault. So they return an error string instead.

Guess which one?

The same asterisk: *.

Three weeks later they add a length limit: passwords longer than 256 bytes burn CPU. Anything longer is rejected. And since it’s an error, crypt() returns *.

2016

OpenSSH fixes a timing attack (CVE-2016-6210). If a user doesn’t exist, the server still hashes the password with a fake/borrowed salt so an attacker can’t tell valid usernames by response time.

2022

Alpine Linux changes the locked root password in /etc/shadow from ! to * so SSH keys work properly on cloud images.

… and the loop closes!

You connect over SSH as root (whose shadow entry is *).

You type any password longer than 256 characters (e.g. 300 As).

crypt() hits the length limit → returns * → OpenSSH compares it with the value in the database → that value is also * → you’re in as root.

That chain took 46 years (!!!) to complete.

Every individual change was reasonable. Together they produced a perfect * == * authentication bypass (CVE-2026-123158, nicknamed *sshole). Fixed in OpenSSH 10.6p2 and Alpine packages.
author: officer_secret
quoted_text:
🚨 Critical OpenSSH flaw allows passwordless account access using any password over 256 characters

https://t.co/gILS1Dxn1w

A newly disclosed vulnerability dubbed *sshole has been discovered in OpenSSH installations using musl libc, potentially allowing attackers to bypass authentication and gain access to accounts that should reject password logins entirely.

The flaw affects certain configurations of Alpine Linux, OpenWrt, Buildroot, and Yocto where PAM is disabled and password authentication remains enabled. Under specific conditions, attackers can authenticate to locked accounts using arbitrary passwords between 257 and 1,024 characters.

The researcher demonstrated that affected Alpine Linux cloud images could allow attackers to gain root privileges through a passwordless administrative account.

OpenSSH 10.6p2 addresses the issue. Administrators are urged to update immediately or disable SSH password authentication until patches can be applied.

quoted_text:
The markets NUKED again and X will have you believe AI will be shut down by the Democrats

I don't see the end of AI at all, I see an IRRATIONAL selloff

In these moments it's best to RELAX and take a LOOK at the data

Here's my thoughts on macro, sentiment and midterms:

MIDTERMS:

The big change obviously is the Blue Tsunami and the fear of dems wanting to shutdown AI and stop the build out of data centers. While this may be true of the extreme dems, it's not the reality of the majority.

What the dems want are data center companies to support the towns they build in, pay for their own power, and not get subsidized. That's reasonable, and a lot of it is already happening

Data centers are the only growing construction sector in the US, bringing in billions in tax revenue and hundreds of thousands of jobs. Democrats aren't going to throw that away. They'll flex their power and use it as a bargaining chip to make their share and HOPEFULLY create better conditions for their citizens

Some projects may get delayed, but hyperscalers and other companies can work around that by building in other states, paying for onsite power, or paying the towns. The cost to build will now go up though it's very likely companies that already have power and permits just gained even more pricing power

People aren't going to use AI less because Democrats won. The demand is still there, so the revenue is still there, and companies still need compute. We have not overbuilt like 1999, and this is not a 2021 bubble with no users/revenue. We're still underbuilding versus demand

SENTIMENT:

Today was also a deleveraging event combined with programmatic selling. That's what happens when markets move this fast. It triggers even more selling

The VIX spiked 69% at the high today and as the saying goes, when the VIX is high, it's time to BUY. That doesn't mean we already hit the bottom, but things are clearly getting very irrational at this point

This is happening at multi-decade lows in valuations for a lot of these companies, especially the semis. Buying great companies at great multiples during extreme fear is 99% of the time a winning strategy (this is exactly why I bought more $NVDA today).

MACRO:

While prices have tanked over the last couple of weeks, long-term yields, oil, and inflation expectations have come down too, all while the economy and earnings have shown strength. Is this really how a stock market meltdown should form?

We use a propriety data set called The Milk Road Macro Index, which combines more than 20 indicators into one signal for when to take risk or protect capital. It has been calling for RISK-OFF since early September. This allowed our analysts to raise some cash during September (thankfully)

This week, it has sharply turned the other way and jumped out of risk-off and into caution, which tells me that once this irrational sentiment clears, the underlying macro has actually improved significantly. While it's still not hitting full Risk-on, it could hit it any day now

I have no idea how long this meltdown will take or if it gets worse from here. But we have an improving macro backdrop and an irrational selloff from a specific event that is now behind us.

These are the moments that our process says to buy, so that's exactly what I'm doing today. I'm buying great companies at low multiples during peak fear. While its super painful to do right now, it's almost always the best possible decision you can look back on in 6-12months

If you want to see how I'm allocating through this, my real-time portfolio is here: https://t.co/NyRpAKYOwu

text:
One of the interesting things I noticed in this article was that 50% of sequencer fees will be used for buybacks, so we pulled some preliminary onchain data to see what these kinetiq:native buybacks may look like across various scenarios

We sampled ~23K live Elysium transactions from the past hour, and obviously annualizing launch-day data overstates things, so treat these as an upper-bound snapshot, not a run rate:

• ~9.8M tx/day pace, already above Robinhood Chain (~6M) and Base (~8.6M)
• ~$31K/day in sequencer fees at that pace, or ~$5M/yr in KNTQ buybacks (~4% of mcap) if it somehow held all year
• 57% of transactions come from bot/MM wallets, but they pay only 10% of fees
• DEX swaps are 9% of transactions but 61% of fees, and 75% of all fees are priority tips

Launch-day tip activity is the part least likely to last. The base fee pays only ~$0.0008 per tx, so once the launch rush cools, ~$1M to $1.5M/yr in buybacks is perhaps a more realistic steady state. If Elysium can hold 20M tx/day with competitive blockspace, that grows to ~$11M/yr, about 9% of KNTQ’s market cap

also unclear what percent of sequencer revenue if any arbitrum gets given its an arbitrum orbit chain

It's only day one, so we’ll revisit once there are a few weeks of data, especially after their EL1Read/EL1Write upgrade goes live (~4 weeks post-mainnet), which lets Elysium contracts read HyperCore order books natively and write orders directly to HyperCore. That’s when the prop AMMs and market makers that would drive sustainable fee volume should actually show up which could potentially be a big driver of sequencer revenue

text:
At Zerion, we stand with @GrapheneOS. Security reporting needs facts, not sensational headlines.

“Police cracked GrapheneOS” oversimplifies what has actually been reported.

According to the Joint Defense Team, the Dutch reseller case involved a modified fork with remote device management (MDM) and missing security updates. That does not demonstrate a compromise of current, official GrapheneOS.

The German Pixel 8a case is separate: investigators reportedly extracted data from a seized device, but the method, patch level and whether it ran genuine GrapheneOS remain unclear. Neither “everything is cracked” nor “unhackable” is a responsible conclusion.

Be cautious with cheap “secure Pixels” advertised on Snapchat and other social platforms. A GrapheneOS logo does not prove what software is installed or who controls its updates and remote management.

Claims that authorities are distributing pre-compromised Pixels through resellers remain unverified. Suspicion is not evidence.

Use the official installer, relock the bootloader, verify the installation and keep your device updated.

We support @GrapheneOS and its work to protect user privacy. Judge security by evidence not fear or sales pitches.

Zerion

2026.11.06
Global footwear manufacturer Changshin INC. plans to adopt artificial intelligence (AI) and data platforms from Palantir Technologies to integrate information and workflows spanning footwear development, sample planning and factory production. The companies recently signed a partnership agreement to deploy Palantir's data operations platform, Foundry, and its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) across Changshin's development and production operations.

According to Palantir, the partnership is one of the outcomes of its recent AgentCamp program, which allows participants to build AI agents and apply them to real-world business tasks. Changshin said its engineers used company data to develop and demonstrate initial workflows during AgentCamp, confirming their potential to improve operational efficiency.

Building on those results, the companies plan to connect decisions made during product development with factory production planning and execution. Changshin aims to consolidate information and feedback across the entire process to identify problems earlier, reduce inefficiencies in handoffs between departments and incorporate production results into future decision-making.

Palantir emphasized that Changshin will retain control over how AI is applied at every stage.

Palantir Foundry is a data operations platform that integrates fragmented enterprise data and connects it to analytics, decision-making and operational execution. One of Palantir's flagship products, it primarily serves private-sector businesses and enables operational teams and developers to work from a shared data model.

Palantir AIP structures enterprise data and business rules into an ontology and securely integrates large language models (LLMs). This enables companies to develop and operate AI agents and applications for practical business use.

text:
It’s abundantly clear that the U.S. intel community not only knew about all of this for a long time but also most likely briefed Jensen and used him to gather intel on China’s efforts to evade sanctions. 

Supporting evidence for this theory is that the media has had images and videos of them together for a very long time and Trump and Marco Rubio were briefed on this a full year ago. Additionally, Trump not only met with Jensen several times after he even allowed him to travel on Air Force One to a state dinner in China. There is no shot whatsoever the secret service or the intel community would have allowed someone who was that compromised to be this close to the president even if there was the smallest chance that he could be relaying information to foreign actors. 

The most likely scenario is that Jensen was notified and briefed on the threat before and the intel community thought it was more advantageous to use the opportunity for counter espionage and potential sabotage. The U.S. has a history of doing operations like this, if you take a look at stuxnet, the virus designed to sabotage Iran’s nuclear reactors by targeting their industrial controllers, it took the Iranians over a year to figure out they were being sabotaged and that was with backing of the entire state resources and its engineering talent. 

With GPUs it’s harder to discover these bugs, in fact it could take forever to figure out. A bit flip here and there, a small math mistake here, intermittent thermal throttling, bad telemetry reports etc. you would be flying blind for a looooong time and there are even ways to build in anti reverse engineering measures if a card was pulled out on a bench to be tested. 

That being said I think the Chinese eventually got wise to this and with the change in the house and senate they thought it was the opportune time to let the cat out the bag. It’s telling that Jensen will be testifying to the house in a closed door meeting. Sadly he still needs to claim he was “cheating” to the public as admitting to working with the intelligence community to sabotage a foreign country would be 10x worse for diplomatic relations and for Nvidia. 

Even though I’m not his biggest fan, if what I think it’s true you can’t call Jensen anything other than a real American patriot. It must be very hard to sacrifice your public image and your families peace for the country.

quoted_text:
New @greenpillnet special season out now! 🌐

The first episode kicks off a new Greenpill mini-series on Economic Media.  We’re exploring how protocols, ledgers, AI agents and computational systems are becoming the media through which economic coordination is recorded, interpreted and governed.

This guest season is by @econaut6 , Jorge López, and Jonathan Beller of the @ecospaceagency.  They are exploring what changes if the economy is itself a medium: how screens and platforms turned meaning-making into value extraction, why accounting has a grammar of its own, and why blockchain distributed computation without distributing economic agency. 

Who gets to define an asset, recognize a contribution or change a network's rules, and what would it take for care, community priorities and long-excluded people to count?

Along the way they discuss whether the economy is a medium at all, or an ecology of media, and close on why the series is a laboratory: an experimental, interdisciplinary space for building economic literacy and new practices.

author: ryanberckmans
quoted_text:
1. Intro

Vitalik recently wrote about where the EF should go; Aya added a note to explain how we got here, and why. I’ll write about the execution.

We now have enough clarity to stop treating “what is the EF for?” as an open-ended question. Our mandate is clear: The EF exists to ensure Ethereum is, becomes, and remains real permissionless infrastructure for self-sovereignty: censorship (and capture) resistant, free and open source, private, and secure; and capable of supporting sovereignty-preserving coordination at scales where trusted institutions hitherto have been unavoidable.

The following are my thoughts on some of the points that follow from the mandate and how we are translating it to action. But first, a short reminder about

2. What the EF is not for

We are not here to optimize for EF importance, corpo/pol appeal, or ecosystem popularity. We are also not here to please short-term speculators, prop up TBTF neo-SIFIs, market every app on Ethereum, help anyone look good to their crypto or investor friends, or provide on-demand entertainment for dinner parties and private retreats.

3. What the EF is for: Eliminating weaknesses

We are here to defensively strengthen places where Ethereum is, or can still become, extractive, totalizing, or vulnerable to cartel or state capture, or authoritarian tools of surveillance or coercion.

We will base our actions on a full examination of what Ethereum is and can be at the protocol layer (what is actually running as “Ethereum”), the access layer (what users use to interact with the protocol), the user layer (the end-users who need and will need Ethereum), and the institutional layer (the intermediated paths that scale self-sovereign usage).

The EF exists to harden every surface of Ethereum, including those where Ethereum can remain formally permissionless while becoming practically captured. Some obvious surfaces are the transaction pipeline, staking and network security, access layer standards and interfaces, self-sovereignty norms, privacy expectations, institutional adoption patterns, and social layer governance processes. The primary concerns are similar across most of them: does the status quo and its future trajectory minimize trusted dependencies, minimize points of leverage and capture vectors, make user privacy the default, preserve exit, and make trust assumptions legible?

The work starts with the EF itself. We are moving compensation and major financial relationships toward ETH and mandate-compliant Ethereum-native stables, with exceptions where positive law or unavoidable operational constraints require exceptions. Rather than a purity ritual or instruction for people to take unmanaged personal risk, it is robustness, alignment, and product pressure. If the EF’s work is to make Ethereum usable as infrastructure for self-sovereignty, everyone at the EF will increasingly live inside the constraints of the system the EF exists to improve: wallet UX, volatility, accounting, privacy gaps, payment friction, stablecoin trust assumptions, recovery, dependency risk, etc. If we can’t use these tools ourselves, it is unrealistic to expect others to. Ethereum is already mature; those who do not depend on the user-facing stack have no business trying to shape its future, at any layer.

The transaction pipeline is next. Preventing toxic MEV capture is core EF work, not a peripheral market-structure concern. Transaction supply, ordering, inclusion, block construction, propagation, and settlement are part of Ethereum’s neutrality boundary. Some MEV may persist as an adversarial phenomenon the protocol contains, but it must be absolutely minimized and, for that to be possible, we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence by its beneficiaries.

If credibly neutral execution is subverted by privileged orderflow, cartelized builders, trusted relays, opaque routing, or validators outsourcing into a narrow supply chain, Ethereum will look permissionless while users experience it as intermediated at the moment value moves. EF protocol work will therefore prioritize lower barriers to block building and validation, stronger inclusion guarantees, reduced extraction opacity, competitive transaction pipelines, user-facing legibility of trust assumptions, and more aggressively exploring the open orderflow solution space.

None of this is simple. A good solution in one place can aggravate problems elsewhere. FOCIL is good for censorship resistance, but it may introduce more cross-block MEV. While ePBS solves the relayer trust problem, we must make sure that its implementation does not inadvertently obstruct long-term solutions to even larger problems. It would be unacceptable, for example, if ePBS enshrining the builder economy ends up making it harder to reduce reliance on the private orderflow that has emptied out the public mempool. Encrypted mempools may not only reduce pre-execution transparency and pending orderflow visibility, but also shift competitive advantage to new privileged actors, including specialized hardware operators in some designs, while adding protocol complexity.

In order to avoid wasting time playing whack-a-mole, we must commit to solving the extraction problem at a whole system scale. Doing so will require creativity, courage, and the understanding that failure to solve this problem is unacceptable. If we fail, we will have left in place an unnecessary barrier to institutional adoption, but, more importantly, we will also have surrendered a core part of the promise of Ethereum - the replacement of extractive middlemen with permissionless, credibly neutral infrastructure and competitive markets. That must not happen.

MEV is likely to be the next major front in the cypherpunk war. We must set ourselves up to win here.

Privacy is just as fundamental. A public ledger without serious privacy defaults is a surveillance substrate with settlement guarantees. That is not an acceptable end state for the world computer. Unconditional privacy will be readily available across Ethereum, with programmability on top for selective disclosure, proofs, auditability, compliance logic, reputation, governance, identity, and other constraints chosen by users and their communities. The temporal order matters: unconditional privacy must exist first, opt-in constraints come second.

It is also important to avoid forcing users to assemble a fragile stack of special wallets, RPCs, bridges, apps, compliance providers, and operational habits to attain privacy. Deep privacy must be more secure than this. Privacy is a condition for Ethereum’s viability as freedom-respecting coordination infrastructure and as such must be robust.

Staking must be treated as protocol infrastructure risk. Staking is not merely a yield product, and liquid staking is not merely an app-layer market. If stake, liquidity, validator access, DeFi collateral, and governance influence concentrate around a small set of issuers or operators, Ethereum’s security layer becomes vulnerable to capture through capture of the economic layer around it. EF will support research, specifications, and designs that keep staking permissionless, private where possible, plural in operation, and resistant to intermediaries becoming permanent control points.

The access interfaces are where users access either the protocol directly or through intermediated defaults. The primary problem to solve here is not getting Ethereum into more rooms directly, but making its users, both end users and institutions, more self-sovereign and less susceptible to coercion, and avoiding normalization of soft coercion in exchange for reach. EF will not help Ethereum become more acceptable by sanding off the properties that make it uniquely valuable. Ethereum does not need to become another permissioned settlement backend with better branding. It needs to show, in production, that self-sovereign coordination at scale is possible.

Across Ethereum, the EF’s defensive work seeks to ensure that Ethereum is infrastructure people can still use when counterparties fail, platforms censor, governments overreach, intermediaries extract, and coordination problems become infeasible for trusted systems to handle. A core part of that is to make that infrastructure secure and robust against capture at every layer wherever capture opportunities can hide.

4. What the EF is also for: Seizing opportunities

Shoring up the fundamentals is not enough. Ethereum’s potential is still largely unrealized, but that does not mean that the path ahead is going to be straight. Opportunities must be seized when the time is right. At this moment in time, a number are visible, including:

* Ethereum becoming the first quantum-resistant global infrastructure. Ethereum researchers will lead the post-quantum cryptographic migration before the threat becomes urgent, not after it becomes a governance emergency. That means hardening Ethereum’s cryptographic foundations while there is still time to design carefully. The same applies to other long-horizon risks, where waiting for market demand means waiting until the window for principled design has already closed.

* Verifiably self-sovereign stack, from soup to nuts, whether local or remote, with no censorship or extraction openings: browsers, wallets, intents, broadcasts, orderflow, inclusion, block construction, proposal, proving, exit, and recovery. Minimal MEV, and zero toxic MEV entrenchment, either in or around the protocol. No execution layer that is formally permissionless but practically gatekept by privileged supply chains. If there’s a funnel towards an extractive private lane, there’s other options that keep the game live. The goal is not only to prevent extraction or capture, but to make credibly neutral execution competitive enough that serious users prefer it.

* Making ETH normal digital cash: a private, dignity-respecting, debasement-resistant and surveillance-resistant medium of exchange and store of value, as well as the native asset of private computation and private coordination for both humans and their agents. If Ethereum can make private economic life and private institutional life possible without routing users back through the friction and potential abuse of custodians, surveillance vendors, or permissioned ledgers with softer branding, as well as provide a venue for secure and competitive machine economics, the value unlocks will be immense.

* Personal wallets with personal AI agents that users can actually own and run on their own personal computers. Not your keys, not your coins; not your model, not your mind. As agents become interfaces for more economic and social action, the question of who owns the wallet, the model, the memory, the policy, and the signing authority becomes an existential question about sovereignty instead of UX details - we are all users above any other roles, and no one at EF will forget this.

* Institutional and enterprise use cases where Ethereum wins by not disappearing into an invisible backend, gatekept by intermediaries or terrible UX, and by not compromising into a compliant fintech rail with web3 branding. Rather, we will win through proving that credibly neutral infrastructure can handle disintermediated coordination so competitively that trusted intermediaries have to meet Ethereum users on Ethereum’s terms.

* Security-preserving scaling. L2s and related infrastructure will be able to meet institutional-level needs without accepting dependencies on closed operators, opaque sequencing, custodial UX, or upgrade committees that users cannot realistically exit. Scale is not throughput alone. Scale is the guaranteed availability of self-sovereignty under real load. 

We are ensuring Ethereum remains the hardest bedrock for settlement, local and worldwide; and beyond that, a civilizational ledger and execution substrate to stand the test of time. When future civilizations speak of the infrastructure they inherited from the Antiquity of the Information Age, their first example should be Ethereum.

Ethereum will outlast all of us. More than enough people watching understand this. Many wondered why it needed saying at all, but it did. If you don't believe us or don't get it, we don't have time to try to convince you, sorry.

5. Addressing departures

There has been a lot of online speculation about departures from EF, both before and after the mandate. Some people resigned, others were terminated. Some departures were about strategy, some about role fit, some about normal institutional change, and some simply about people deciding that their best work for Ethereum should happen somewhere else. We will not litigate individual personnel matters on Twitter. That is the default because it is better for EF, better for the people involved, and better for Ethereum. People who contributed through EF deserve dignity on the way out. They do not deserve to have their employment history turned into factional content.

Where possible, we have let people describe their departures in their own words as a matter of courtesy, and not concession. If public claims materially mislead people about EF’s direction, decision-making, or mandate, we may correct the record at the level of policy, process, and institutional facts. We still will not turn personal files into public spectacle.

Ethereum is permissionless. People may disagree, criticize, compete, fork, and build elsewhere. We intend to keep exits dignified and expect others to do the same. It will suffice to say that we are thankful for what all contributors have built; we will continue to do work Ethereum needs. 

6. Addressing EF spinouts

Some work should and will leave the EF in the months to come. We hope and expect this process to result in some excellent work being done in service of scaling self-sovereign adoption, but we also must take care lest it becomes an abdication of responsibility or an excuse for undisciplined spending. Some work is not mandate-compatible and should not be carried forward with EF funds or EF endorsement, either inside or outside the Foundation.

The efforts carried out by the spinouts will vary widely. Some efforts will leave EF because another org would be a better home for them; others will leave because markets should decide on their worth. Some will leave because they are not compatible with the direction set out in the mandate; others because they are useful but not EF work. 

Just as a spinout is not automatically good because it reduces EF headcount, former EF affiliation is not a claim on EF funding. The question we ask when deciding on funding is not “did this come from the EF?” But, rather the questions that should be asked about all external funding:

“Is this work mandate-critical? Would the EF do this work internally if it had the organizational and financial capacity? Is there no better natural home? Can the external party execute without increasing capture risk, private extraction, opacity, or dependence? Does supporting it reduce Ethereum’s dependence on the EF over time, without prematurely transferring resources and legitimacy to new organizations and thereby risking operational failure or mission drift?”

EF funding for work being done externally can be appropriate when it is a capacity solution for mandate work - work the EF should responsibly want done; work that protects CROPS; work that advances self-sovereignty and scales it; essential work that no actor can or will reliably do without EF funding; and work that can be scoped, reviewed, and held accountable without creating a permanent dependency.

Such funding is not appropriate when it is a lazy continuity payment, a friendship payment, a reputational hedge, a way to avoid making a hard decision, or a way to support work that is not compatible with the mandate.

EF has finite funds, finite legitimacy, and a specific mandate. We will spend all three as if they matter. When we say “EF is one of many nodes”, we mean that we intend to be one of many nodes working to keep self-sovereignty and its scaling the North Star, and working to keep CROPS the undisplaceable first-class properties of the network. We don’t mean that we will support orgs or projects with different priorities. Diversity that leads to ecosystem resilience, coordination cost right-sizing, and better decision-making is good. Diversity that leads to mission drift is not.

We are not neutral on the direction Ethereum takes. CROPS are not just things we “believe in”, they are characteristics we understand must be thoughtfully prioritized at every fork for Ethereum to realize its potential. We are partisans for and builders of something of such incredible neutrality that it will fundamentally reshape the world we live in; we wish to work with everyone committed to this shared purpose.

text:
There is one thing I would like to say.

My expertise is in semiconductor technology and the semiconductor industry. I have a PhD in semiconductor engineering and work as a design engineer in Silicon Valley. I also run a community with hundreds of semiconductor professionals. Through seminars and conversations with people in the industry, I continue to study and research where the technology and the industry are heading.

The articles I started writing earlier this year have helped many readers, and my X and Substack have attracted more attention than I expected. I am always grateful for that.

I have my own views as an individual investor, and I share opinions on certain companies and industries. However, analyzing a company’s technology and competitiveness is different from accurately predicting stock prices or knowing exactly when to buy and sell. My expertise lies in the former. I cannot claim to be good at the latter. If I were, I would probably be working on Wall Street in New York rather than in Silicon Valley.

That is why I always mention NFA and DYOR when sharing my investment views. My judgment has limitations, and you should examine the reasoning and make your own decisions. In fact, when someone recklessly tells people to buy or sell with absolute certainty, I firmly believe that person is a fraud.

The same applies to how I view the memory industry.

I remain optimistic about the memory business. Based on what I see and hear, my experience working in the industry, and my technical understanding, I still see plenty of reasons for optimism in demand trends and the structural changes in memory technology. That is why I do not change my view of the industry simply because memory stocks fall. If you criticize me for discussing the memory business when I could not even predict the selloff, I do not have much to say in response. Sorry, but that simply is not what I am good at…

If changes in supply, demand, or technological competitiveness overturn the basis of my view, I will change my opinion. NVHBM is what I am watching most closely right now. I plan to have more conversations with memory experts toward the end of the year and share my insights.

So, coming back to the question, if you ask me, “Memory stocks have fallen this much, and you are still optimistic about memory?” my answer is yes, because the industry fundamentals I see still support that view. I will not pretend to know when the stocks will rebound. In the meantime, I will keep researching the memory business and checking whether the basis for my view still holds.

Going forward, I will not praise a company simply because it sponsors me, nor will I write only favorable articles about a company simply because I own its stock. I will also not change the basis of my analysis merely because a company’s stock price rises or falls.

What I want to offer here is evidence and perspective that help you understand changes in semiconductor technology and the industry, so you can make your own judgments. You do not have to agree with my conclusions. But if my writing makes technology a little easier to understand, gives you another question to ask about a company or industry, or helps you reassess your investment decisions using more concrete evidence, then I believe my research is doing its job.

Thank you.

text:
Polymarket或许正在往IPO的道路上走，但是，100%落定了吗？我觉得没有。

既然大家都觉得现在是背后的大股东“当家作主”，那么，其最后就肯定会朝着利益出发。当TGE得到的估值比IPO更高，让股权投资者更容易退出的时候，Polymarket的主要股东会选择TGE。

当然，前提条件有：
1、加密货币回归新一轮大牛市，比如BTC突破10万，市场风险偏好提高使得项目估值提升
2、Polymarket和Kalshi在跟各个州进行的法律诉讼中，发生重大不利判罚，导致IPO路线艰难
3、被民主党领导的众议院和参议院调查政治、体育两种事件合约的合法合规

民主党上台后，IPO的策略确实有点难执行，因为背后的股东好像跟民主党没有什么关系，而且，最关键的是里面牵扯了特朗普家族的利益。

退一步看，就算达成IPO，市场对这个赛道的叙事也已经去魅，在经历了几十亿美金的融资和几年的发展之后，所谓互联网真相器的叙事并没有完全实现，其挣钱的逻辑还是跟传统博彩市场一样：体育博彩。

所以，IPO后能够保持200亿市值？应该有点牵强。

我不是想说服自己和大家继续去刷交易，也不是贬低这个赛道，而是客观地分析当前的形势。或许未来预测市场会突破瓶颈取得更大的成功，但是，至少当前一两年内很难完全实现互联网真相叙事。

当然，TGE的概率并不好判断，因为非常多的因素不可控。

其实，在世界杯之前我就发文分析过polymarket的处境：
代币是kalshi做不到的，代币就是polymarket独有的核武器。在世界杯前进行TGE，利用好代币在社区空投中的作用，然后其全球平台可以完美承接世界杯这个机会，把用户、交易、利润数据大幅提高，重新抢回龙头地位。

然后宣布第二阶段的空投计划，perps被包含在第二阶段的空投计划之中，因为，第一阶段空投的造富效应，perps将迅速取代hyperliquid成功龙头。

2026年世界杯带来超预期数据，以及第二阶段的空投计划让perps交易量暴涨，这两个事件都将使得polymarket稳坐赛道龙头。这也就为polymarket us挣多美国市场提供了更多的资金支持和争取了更多的发展时间。也为2027/2028的IPO奠定了漂亮的业绩数据。

不管是选择IPO还是选择TGE，都应该重视世界杯。但是，坦白讲，它们最终并没有利用好世界杯这个机会。

最后，因为它们给出过很多的空投预期，然后又主动把这些预期打破，而且在费用方面似乎没有跟社区/用户进行更多的沟通。这让用户匪夷所思，很难看懂当前的发展路线和未来要走向何方。

希望他们能够懂用户，也让用户看懂它。

quoted_text:
I’ve come to the realization that it’s not worth spending any more of my time trying to farm the Polymarket airdrop.

That said, the market is still pricing in some value, with $POLY TGE odds remaining relatively healthy. I wanted to share my thoughts on why that might be and what the market is pricing in.

The Endgame

It shouldn't come as a surprise that Polymarket and Kalshi are looking to IPO before the US elections. After 2028, they could face significant legal scrutiny, especially at the state level, given that a substantial portion of their volume comes from sports betting.

The Competition

With sports and esports markets accounting for an increasingly large share of volume, the recent fee increases make competition even fiercer. These markets are also the easiest to provide liquidity to.

This is similar to what happened with crypto exchanges, which launched tokens and offered fee discounts to attract and retain users. It also validates the idea that a token and a stock can coexist.

The Lack of Goodwill and PMF

The community has been very tolerant of Polymarket's buggy codebase and reliance on a third-party oracle despite all the money they've raised.

Although the team has made some significant product improvements recently, I think we're at a point where Polymarket has a goodwill problem more than a product problem. They've teased a token airdrop multiple times over the past two years and still haven't delivered.

The sad reality is that some projects can afford not to deliver on their promises. Pumpfun, for example, has already generated more revenue than it raised in funding.

Polymarket isn't in the same position. I'm not saying there's no product-market fit, but it isn't strong enough yet to make the business as sustainable or scalable as it needs to be.

The Bailout

VCs have invested over $2B in Polymarket, and the company is now valued at $20B. At some point, they'll want to realize their profits.

The path forward is supposedly an IPO, but the current metrics and growth trends are nowhere near enough to justify that valuation. It's also unclear whether they can raise more money, and there's little indication that things are improving beyond the recent product fixes.

The platform has generated only around $100M in cumulative net revenue.

In fact, if the VCs had put the money invested in Polymarket into US Treasuries instead, they could have earned more than the platform has generated in revenue. And since the beginning of the year, Polymarket hasn't been growing anywhere near as fast as you'd expect from one of the biggest players in the prediction market space.

What's Being Priced In

I think the market is pricing in a bailout in the form of a token that would not only give VCs an alternative way to exit or hedge their positions before an IPO, but also give Polymarket the exponential growth it needs to get there.

It's obviously much easier to sell that story when the platform is growing like crazy. A token could give Polymarket that hockey-stick growth before going public.

But what would that actually look like?

The Ideal Scenario

This part is obviously speculative, but I'd imagine something along these lines:

> The international platform is separated from the US entity and placed under a nonprofit organization.
>The token is announced, followed by the airdrop.
> A second points program is announced, running for a year or longer.
> Revenue-funded buybacks are introduced, with no long-term commitment to them, similar to what Pumpfun has done.

Just look at the TVL and open interest that perp DEXs have attracted through points programs. Something like this could easily give Polymarket the hockey-stick growth it needs.

Again, they wouldn't be doing this because they care about the community. They'd be doing it to make the stock and prediction market story easier to sell, giving users something back in exchange for extracting even more value in the future. The platform's fees are already very high.

Which Way, Western Man?

It's clear that Polymarket either isn't ready to go public with its plans or wants to keep its options open.

We've seen Shayne talk vaguely about an on-chain asset without explaining what it might look like. Is he talking about an independent token, or something pegged to the stock?

All of this comes at a heavy cost though, as more and more liquidity leaves the platform every day.

Token teases have reached a point where they no longer seem to help revive volume. Instead, they're damaging the platform's reputation without having any meaningful impact on volume anymore.

At some point in the near future, Polymarket won't be able to kick the can down the road any longer (unlike OpenSea). And it'll become increasingly obvious whether they're ever going to launch a token.

Anthropic 发了新模型，OpenAI 发了台游戏机：Codex 版 Chromatic 掌机开卖，200 美元，用 Codex 自己做 Game Boy 游戏

11 月 9 日，Anthropic 发布了 Claude Fable 5.2 和 Mythos 5.2。同一天，OpenAI 在自家周边商店 Supply Co. 上架了一台掌机：ModRetro Chromatic 的 Codex 版，售价 200 美元。

Chromatic 是 ModRetro 做的复古掌机，这家公司由 Oculus 创始人 Palmer Luckey 创办。它能直接插原版 Game Boy 和 Game Boy Color 卡带玩，2.56 英寸屏幕，分辨率 160×144，和当年的 Game Boy Color 一样。Codex 版是透明外壳，盒子里带一张可以写入自制游戏的卡带。

【能干什么】

在 Codex 里装上 ModRetro Chromatic 插件，用一句话描述想做的游戏，Codex 帮你做出来。ModRetro 上手指南里的示例是：“做一个小探索游戏，园丁收集三颗种子，种下后打开一扇门。”接着可以让它加场景、画会走路的像素小人、换一套月夜配色，也可以让它检查美术素材有没有超出 Game Boy 的硬件限制。

游戏工程用的是 GB Studio，一款免费开源的 Game Boy 游戏制作工具，Codex 做完的东西可以在里面接着手动改。最后输出一个 ROM 文件，也就是游戏本体，可以自己玩，也可以发给别人。

试玩有三种方式：在电脑上的浏览器模拟器里玩，哪里不满意就让 Codex 改；从电脑把游戏串流到掌机上，试按键手感、画面和声音；或者把游戏写进卡带，不连电脑也能随身玩。写卡带前要先升级掌机固件，再用 Codex 版附带的激活码开启开发者模式。

OpenAI 的页面上放了三款用 Codex 做的游戏：消除类的 Seedy's Sweet Garden，打怪升级的地牢冒险 Hollow Descent，跟着箭头跳舞的音游 Codex Dance。

【不买掌机能不能玩，买的话多少钱】

不买也能玩。插件在 Codex 桌面版的插件页搜索安装，ChatGPT 免费账号也能用 Codex，只是额度有限。做出来的游戏在浏览器模拟器里就能玩。OpenAI 开发者网站上还有一批用 Codex 做的 Game Boy Color 游戏，浏览器里免费玩，也能下载 ROM。

想在真机上玩，才需要买。ModRetro 官网上，标准版 Chromatic 卖 199.99 美元，换蓝宝石玻璃屏是 299.99 美元，10 月推出的透明版是 149.99 美元，三款都送一张 Tetris 卡带。Codex 版 200 美元，包含一张可写入的卡带和开发者模式激活码。配套的保护壳和额外的卡带在 Supply Co. 单卖。

Codex 版只发货到美国、加拿大、澳大利亚、新西兰、日本、英国和欧盟，不包括中国大陆。

【它从哪来】

这台掌机最早是 9 月 29 日 OpenAI DevDay 开发者大会的现场礼物。当时参会者每人领到一台限量透明版 Chromatic，ModRetro 和 OpenAI 同时宣布合作，放出了用 Codex 做 Game Boy 游戏的这套流程。现在 OpenAI 换了新外观，把它作为 Supply Co. 的新品重新开卖。

text:
Stumbled across an incredible LA Times article from 1996 - "The Dirty Secret About the Net" 

It was written about the nascent consumer Internet, but you could replace "web" with "agents" and get a perfect mirror of the current discourse

The author's predictions (he was the paper's tech editor): 

- The time for startups had passed, and Microsoft would own the Internet market (Google was founded two years later) 
- It would take more than a decade for the Internet to become a consumer phenomenon, if it ever did (it took <5 years)
- Privacy and security concerns + complicated setup meant that the web would only appeal to high income, highly educated coastal elites
- Infrastructure was "groaning under the weight of the huge traffic increases" - this would be very slow to fix, and would significantly limit adoption
- Online shopping showed "few signs of taking off" - even if payment issues were solved, retail shopping was too entertaining for users to default to the Internet
- Making money would be near-impossible - consumers would not pay subscriptions, and the Internet's reach was not enough to generate real advertising revenue

My favorite one-liner: "Many new businesses, like the huge online bookstore Amazon, will find a niche." 

...as well as the fact that the author's prior piece was "The Fall of Apple Computer"

quoted_text:
Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

quoted_text:
短期流动性危机导致AI股大跌，并不是因为AI基本面出问题，那些瞎鸡巴乱编的故事！

纽约梅隆银行：为什么最近半导体在财报仍强的时候也会大跌？

因为市场上借短期资金越来越贵。美国政府吸走的钱变多，而银行体系里可用的现金变少了

一、钱为什么变紧了？

1. 美国政府大量借短债。纽约梅隆说，从10月初开始，短期国债净发行增加了超过2,600亿美元。投资者买国债，要拿现金出来，短期资金市场可用的钱就更紧。

2. 财政部账户里存的钱增加。政府借来的钱先进入财政部在美联储的账户。11月3日，当时TGA超过1万亿美元，银行准备金一度低于2.9万亿美元。钱从银行体系流进政府账户，暂时不在市场上周转。

3. 市场借钱成本上升。回购市场的短期借款利率SOFR和TGCR都升到了银行准备金利率之上。机构借隔夜资金比平时更贵，是资金偏紧的信号。

二、什么时候可能改善？

纽约梅隆在11月3日预计，纽约联储可能在11月中旬左右恢复「准备金管理购债」，帮助银行体系补充现金，从而缓解短期融资压力。

纽约梅隆也警告，2027年第一季度如果继续大量发行短债，压力可能再次出现。

三、如何传导到半导体？

市场现金偏紧 → 借钱和融资更贵 → 机构降低风险、减少杠杆 → 卖掉此前持仓最拥挤的AI和半导体 → 股价跌。

同时，大科技和AI数据中心需要借钱建设。信用利差扩大意味着融资更贵，市场就开始担心：如果融资变难，数据中心会不会建得慢一些，芯片订单会不会往后推？股价反映的是未来预期，所以即使今天的订单还很强，股价也会先跌。

아 이게 그 3번인가보다. 오더컷

근데 저 오더컷 중에 1번은 내가 반도체 현장에 있었는데, 그때도 주가가 상승하는데도 공장 건설 속도 늦추라고 발주처에서 오더가 왔었음. 그리고 얼마뒤부터 주가가 나락으로 갔었음. 

지금은 삼성도, 하이닉스도 그럴 징후가 전혀 없고 하루라도 빨리 완성하라고 난리임.

과거 그때와 지금 양상이 좀 다른 것 같긴한데..

똑똑한 형들은 금리가 다시 인상되면서 소비 둔화가 발생되고, AI Capex도 자금 조달 여력이 하락하면서 반도체 숏티지가 시간이 흐르면 하락 할 것이라고.. 그런 말들도 해주더라.

근데 동양의 이 작은 한국에도 내년도부터 1GW 짜리 데이터센터들 물량 터지는데, 다른 나라들이라고 안그럴까.

올해 아시아권역에서 데이터센터 진행중인 물량의 총 합이 4~5GW라고 박람회에서 설명해주더라고, 근데 내년도 지어지는 계획인게 26.5GW임.

민간이 소비를 줄여서.. 핸드폰 안팔려서 난리였던 과거와 지금은 완전히 다른 것 같음.

이번 루트는 가보지 않은 길인 것 같은데, 똑똑한 형들은 고점 지났다고 끝났다구 자꾸 이야기하니깐.... 엄청 신경 쓰이긴 함.

똑똑한 형들이랑 승부 볼 만큼 공부를 하지는 않았지만, 지금도 한국에서 데이터센터 서버 임대료 계속 상승하는 중이고 이쪽도 분명히 숏티지가 있거든. 수요가 공급을 압도하는 상황인데

개발사업자들도 돈은 걱정하지 말고, 전기만 해결하라고 자기들이 자본 조달한다고 난리라니깐.

이게 한국 운영사들만 그런게 아니라, 미국쪽이나 싱가포르쪽 회사들이 한국 건설업체들한테 투자할테니깐, 지어달라고 검토해달라고 한다니깐.

미국에 일시적으로 충격와도, 다른 나라에 지으려는 것 같은데..

이게 한 두달 지나면 뭐 상황 정리가 되지 않을까.

과거에 핸드폰 판매 급감, 노트북 판매 급감해서 반도체 공포가 생기고.. 뭐 그런 상황이랑은 완전 다른 새로운 상황인 것 같은데..

quoted_text:
UPDATE: Scott Galloway reached out to me earlier today and asked me to call him. I'm glad I did.

I've read @profgalloway's books, listened to his podcasts, and appreciated his willingness to confront campus antisemitism and debate people he vigorously disagrees with, including @BenShapiro with comity (and more than a little comedy).

That's why his recent comments about Elon Musk surprised and troubled me.

My central criticism was that Scott called Musk a "traitor to the West" while invoking Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, who were executed for espionage.

I think it was a careless statement, but I don't think Scott is calling for Musk's execution. Too many people on this platform are making that accusation, but it's an oversimplification. He told me he explicitly opposes capital punishment. I still believe the analogy was overblown.

We also discussed what actually happened with Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine. What was restricted, when, by whom, and under whose authority? I agree with him that we need to know what actually happened for transparency's sake. Sunlight is the best disinfectant.

Scott acknowledged that if Musk was legitimately enforcing a commercial agreement, not meddling in wartime policies as a private citizen, the accusation of treachery would be unwarranted. I hope that if that occurs, he will retract it publicly.

We agree that serious accusations require serious evidence.

I raised Scott's role as a UC Regent because I believe those entrusted with governing the best university on the planet deserve particular scrutiny. I never called for his removal, nor do I want him removed.

Scott explained why that framing troubled him. I listened, and I understand his concerns better.

Despite disagreeing with my criticism, Scott offered to defend my academic freedom and my right to criticize him.

As a professor, I teach students to revise their conclusions when confronted with new evidence. Today I was reminded that professors must also reconsider their own approach, too.

I stand by the substance of my criticism. But my tone should have been more collegial.

Our conversation strengthened my respect for Scott's generosity and commitment to the University of California, a system that transformed both our lives. As a two-time native son of the UC system, I think Scott will play a vital role on that august board.

Lastly, and most remarkably, two podcast hosts managed to have a contentious discussion and find common ground without recording another podcast about it.

A first in (unrecorded) history.

author: HarryStebbings
quoted_text:
Honestly, 12 months ago I thought “sovereignty” was a BS marketing message for founders to leverage to get funding.

Now I think it is a strategic imperative and will breed some of the largest companies of our time.

Mistral is the poster child of sovereignty. The last remaining hope for Europe when it comes to frontier model providers.

I sat down with @MistralAI CEO, @arthurmensch to debunk the hype from reality and ask the uncomfortable questions. My notes from the discussion below.

1. Why Energy Is Not the Ultimate Cost That Matters

Energy makes up around 10% of the total cost of ownership of compute, so it is not where most optimization can happen. The cost of energy is not the one thing that matters in the economics of a project.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @alanchanguk @ChaseLochmiller @ZachBDell

2. What Would Mistral Do Differently If They Were Totally Resource-Unconstrained?

Mistral would build much more capacity, with capital as the main bottleneck. Customers are running out of compute, and once one use case scales they need thousands of GPUs rather than eight. Europe does not have enough compute, so Mistral is putting equity to work to build capacity ahead of demand.

Love to hear your thoughts on this, if you were resource unconstrained today, what would you do differently @alexmashrabov @bavaria_kush

3. How the Inference Market Behaves Very Much Like a Commodity Market

On-demand inference behaves like a high-margin commodity market where pricing matters a lot and demand comes from non-committed customers. Mature customers need service level agreements, reserved physical capacity and guarantees on latency and generation speed. The more precisely they describe the shape of their demand, the better Mistral can price it.

What does no one see about the inference market that everyone should see @tuhinone @neilmovva @lqiao

4. Models Have Gotten So Strong They Are Being Treated as Defense Systems

Models are now strong enough to carry out cyberattacks, and the US began banning them outside the country in May. China is also looking at restricting exports beyond a certain threshold. As with any dual-use technology, customers now want security of supply on both infrastructure and model IP.

What does no one see about the future of security that everyone should see @zeyu1337 @nikesharora @pilvar222

5. Will We End Up With a Model Landscape That Has Just Two to Three Providers?

If every company relies on two or three centralized AI providers, those providers gain enormous leverage. They will use the data their systems produce to build better systems and go after their customers' business, an end game Arthur sees as priced in today.

What will the model landscape look like in 5 years @emostaque @AnjneyMidha @mmurphy

6. The Biggest Problem With AI Effectiveness Within Enterprise Today Is...

Most enterprise problems are not well defined, and ambiguous objectives with humans in the loop cannot be solved through self-improving loops. They only get solved by deploying models that interact with people, which is why Mistral uses FDEs to define problems better.

7. Why You Can Go Public in Europe and Negativity Around European Stock Markets Is BS

Mistral can absolutely go public in Europe, because the bottlenecks of 10 years ago are no longer there. There is a huge appetite from investors worldwide to invest in Europe in both private and public equity. Mistral is preparing for the operational constraints of being public while delivering on its commercial milestones.

You think this is true, you really think you can go public in Europe @eldsjal @klarnaseb

text:
Vitalik made an important point this weekend: ETH's value doesn't come from the fee burn. It comes from stability, which comes from decentralization, censorship resistance and security. And "in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued."

We agree, and it applies to every L1.

Stability isn't a slogan. It's earned block by block. IoTeX L1 has been live since April 2019 and has produced more than 54 million blocks since, through every cycle: bull markets, bear markets, exchange collapses. Today it still finalizes a block every 2.5 seconds, instantly.

But stable doesn't mean frozen. The threats ahead are new: AI that finds exploits faster than any human auditor, and quantum computers that will eventually break today's signatures. A chain that wants to stay stable for the next decade has to keep evolving, in the open, before those threats arrive. That's what we're doing.

In that sense, IOTX is a store of value too: its value rests on the stability of the chain underneath it.
author: iotex_io
quoted_text:
Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

Everyone understands the true nature of the threat in moments like that. You don’t have to waste time or energy trying to get people to face reality because we are all living that reality. Petty differences evaporate. Harsh ideological divides disintegrate. Right now we still have hope that unrestricted warfare means we will be spared the bullets and the bombs. But that’s because we don’t know this beast. It’s not the movie we’ve seen so many times.  This performance doesn’t open with the bloodshed - they save it for the final act.

No one can tell you what you do not want to hear. No eyes can see what is lost to the willfully blind. And more than that, we are out of time. 

Figure it out - or not. There is only one truth & none of us can alter it.

text:
The future of software

In the limit, of course, software won't mean anything anymore. Everything digital will be instantly created at will. But in the interim period we'll wander through an increasingly odd in-between age for software. This transition periodwill be defined by three new precepts.

Everflux software - instead of stepping from release to release, months apart, software now evolves continuously.

Software creation has broken the sound barrier of our own keystrokes, and every model release pushes it faster. There is no reason to wait weeks or months for the next release when a single company merges over 30,000 code changes a day. Cyber capabilities are also progressing at an increasing pace. Bug and vulnerability fixes need to ship quickly and continuously. And every piece of software sits in a lattice of dependencies, each one now shipping at a blistering pace. Software will have to move accordingly fast just to keep from breaking as everything around it shifts.

Translucent sources – A new territory has opened between open source and closed source.

Today Claude will happily pick apart any Electron app, and any binary shipped with debug symbols has become a reverse-engineering playground for LLMs. In other words, much so-called closed-source software is now open source in all but name, and keeping code closed makes less and less sense.

Even the notion of IP and copyright is breaking in software: Apps don't even need to be accessed to be reproduced. I'm writing this text on a personal text editor I prompted Claude to vibe-code from a few videos of people demoing editor features they liked. A mere description of the interface is increasingly enough for an LLM to rebuild the internals, whether or not they resemble the original. Software IP seems to be dissolving like cotton candy in a raccoon's paws.

Bespoke features - Now that all software is open source, nothing prevents us from modifying everything.

And personalization is just one prompt and a couple million tokens away, so there is absolutely no reason anymore to wait for someone else to add this feature you want. Everyone becomes their own product manager. Want a search box, an API bridge, a custom button? It's a couple of minutes away, mostly executed in the background of your daily life. Soon we'll want to personalize everything.

A major challenge appears when bespoke features crash into our first tenet: everflux software. How do you customize software without cutting yourself off from upstream? I could fork it for good to add my search box, but I'd lose all future benefit from the software creator, be it new security updates or other updates to the rest of the software. How do you personalize software that was never meant to be personalized, without shouldering all of its future maintenance?

Merge conflicts won't be the exception anymore; they'll be a constant of everflux software. Agents will rebase our personal features onto each new release overnight, and software will look less like a product and more like a living species, evolving through constant mutation.

Image: M.C. Escher, Metamorphosis II, November 1939 - March 1940

text:
Thoughts from Michael Hartnett, BofA | DEM fatale
Zeitgeist quote: "My base case now is AI bust, stocks cause recession, then fiscal crisis. But my predictions mean squat right now and I could be buying chip stocks in another hour."
The AI investment boom is reaching extraordinary proportions. Yet the gap between capital deployment, monetization and investor expectations is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.
A few numbers illustrate the scale:
•$820bn in projected hyperscaler capex in 2026, potentially reaching $1 trillion in 2027.
•$297bn in global AI-related debt issuance year-to-date, compared with approximately $100bn in equity issuance.
•41% of US market capitalization now linked to AI-related companies, highlighting extreme market concentration.
•30% of anticipated new US electricity capacity potentially associated with data centers by 2028.
Three developments stand out.
1Financing is becoming a constraint. "Bond/credit markets want AI capex & issuance momentum to slow." The unprecedented infrastructure buildout increasingly depends on debt markets, making financing conditions and future cash generation critical.
2Political and infrastructure constraints are intensifying. Electricity prices, grid capacity, water consumption and local opposition are transforming data center development from a purely commercial decision into a political issue.
3Investor expectations leave little room for disappointment. "Every bull conviction is dead but one." That remaining conviction is the AI-driven earnings boom. If monetization takes longer than expected, the adjustment in valuations could be significant.
The fundamental distinction is between technological success and investment returns.
AI may genuinely transform entire industries while some of today's largest infrastructure investments fail to generate adequate returns on capital.
The next phase of the AI cycle may therefore reward capital discipline, demonstrable monetization and sustainable free cash flow rather than investment scale alone.
The AI revolution is unlikely to stop. But the economics of financing it may be about to change.

author: Veildotcash
quoted_text:
Unfortunately, we’re winding down @veildotcash.

From today, deposits are disabled. We’ll keep the frontend and relayer running until 21 December 2026. After that, withdrawals will still be possible through the CLI.

I haven’t taken this decision lightly. After two years of building something I’m passionate about, I’ve had to accept that the version of privacy I want to build isn’t scaling.

We’ve had periods of strong usage, but it was never sustained. With Veil, privacy depends on usage. As that declines, the privacy becomes weaker. Over the last few months, the protocol hasn’t been delivering the core value I set out to provide.

Although we didn’t solve what I set out to do, I’m extremely proud I tried to tackle what is still to this day the hardest problem in crypto. Privacy.

Going from a 9–5 to being a crypto founder has been one of the most enjoyable and rewarding things I’ve ever done. I feel lucky to have had the opportunity, which makes this a difficult call to make.

I want to thank Base, the Coinbase team and everyone who held, used or supported Veil for helping me work on it for the last two years. Ultimately, I feel I’ve fallen short of what I set out to do.

The wind down also means our support for the VEIL token ends today, including staking rewards and LP incentives. Treasury tokens will be burned.

Finally, I’m not going anywhere. I’m still bullish on crypto, Ethereum and Base, but I’d be lying if I said I knew what I was building next. Veil has had my full focus until now. Whatever comes next, I want to believe in it as much as I believed in this.
